group.passage: By the mid-2010s, the night train seemed headed for the history books. In 2013 and 2014 alone, overnight lines linking Paris with Madrid, Berlin with Paris, and Amsterdam with Prague were shut down. Travelers had moved to low-cost airlines, cars, high-speed daytime trains and long-distance buses, or coaches, and rail companies saw little point in spending money on new carriages. Night trains are also costly to run. They need special sleeping cars, and each train can usually make only one journey a day. Since few people want to get on or off a train at three o'clock in the morning, the stations along the way add little to ticket sales. When Germany's national railway gave up many of its overnight routes, Austria's national railway, ÖBB, took over several of them, including the line between Munich and Rome. Then the mood began to shift. A movement called flygskam, Swedish for "flight shame," spread from Scandinavia, urging people to choose other ways of getting around. In 2019, Sweden saw a rare fall in air passengers, with domestic air travel down 9 percent. Swedavia, the company that runs ten of the country's airports, linked this to several causes, including a tax on flying, worries about the economy and the debate over the climate. Meanwhile, the European Union declared 2021 the European Year of Rail, and new night routes and modern sleeping cars have since appeared across the continent. For many travelers, the appeal is easy to see: they can board after dinner, sleep in a real bed and wake up in another country. The table suggests another reason why climate-minded travelers are interested. For every kilometer a passenger travels, a domestic flight produces about 246 grams of greenhouse gases, while a trip on Britain's national rail produces about 35. Yet the comeback is far from certain. On busy routes, sleeper fares can rise quickly, and getting new sleeping cars paid for and approved is slow and difficult. If night trains are to become a real alternative to flying, supporters say, they will have to become cheaper than planes.

translation_zh.text:
歐洲夜車的復興

到了 2010 年代中期，夜車似乎就要走入歷史。光是 2013 和 2014 年，連接巴黎與馬德里、柏林與巴黎、阿姆斯特丹與布拉格的夜間路線就都停駛了。旅客已經轉向廉價航空、汽車、日間高速列車和長途巴士（也就是長途客運），鐵路公司也覺得沒有必要花錢買新車廂。

夜車的營運成本也很高。它需要特殊的臥鋪車廂，而且每列火車通常一天只能跑一趟。因為很少人想在凌晨三點上下火車，沿途的車站幾乎沒有增加票房收入。德國國鐵放棄許多夜間路線時，奧地利國鐵 ÖBB 接手了其中幾條，包括慕尼黑到羅馬的路線。

後來，風向開始改變。一個名叫 flygskam（瑞典語「飛行羞恥」）的運動從北歐擴散開來，鼓勵人們選擇其他交通方式。2019 年，瑞典的航空旅客罕見地減少，國內航空旅行少了百分之九。經營該國其中十座機場的公司 Swedavia 把這件事歸因於好幾個原因，包括飛行稅、對經濟的擔憂，以及關於氣候的辯論。同時，歐盟把 2021 年訂為「歐洲鐵路年」，之後新的夜車路線和現代化的臥鋪車廂陸續在歐洲各地出現。對許多旅客來說，夜車的吸引力顯而易見：他們可以吃完晚餐後上車，睡在真正的床上，醒來時已經到了另一個國家。

表格點出了注重氣候的旅客對夜車感興趣的另一個原因。每位乘客每移動一公里，國內航班會產生大約 246 公克的溫室氣體，而搭乘英國國鐵大約只產生 35 公克。然而，夜車的復興還很不確定。在熱門路線上，臥鋪票價可能很快上漲，而為新的臥鋪車廂籌措經費並取得核准，過程既緩慢又困難。支持者說，夜車如果要真正成為飛行以外的選擇，就必須變得比搭飛機便宜。
